title: Output-polynomial vertex enumeration
formal:
Do there exist a uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every rational matrix \(M\) and rational vector \(b\) for which
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Mx\leq b\}
\]
is bounded, \(A\) lists every vertex of \(P\) exactly once and halts in at most \(p(L+S)\) bit operations? Here \(L\) is the complete binary input length and \(S\) is the length of the required exact vertex list in the canonical encoding below. The dimension \(d\) is part of the input. Empty, lower-dimensional and degenerate polytopes are included.
definitions:
The input consists of integers \(m,d\geq1\), an explicitly listed matrix \(M\in\mathbb Q^{m\times d}\) and vector \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\). The inequality \(Mx\leq b\) is coordinatewise. Every rational is represented by a signed integer numerator and a positive denominator in binary, in lowest terms, with no leading zeros; zero has numerator zero and denominator one. Fixed delimiters separate dimensions, entries and rows. The input length \(L\) includes all these symbols. Dimensions are unbounded, and no rank, sparsity, integrality or conditioning restriction is imposed.

A polyhedron is a set described by finitely many closed linear inequalities. The promise here is that it is bounded: there exists a finite real number \(B\) such that \(\|x\|_2\leq B\) for every \(x\in P\). An empty set satisfies this promise. The number \(B\) is neither supplied nor assumed to have a given value. A bounded polyhedron is called a polytope. Redundant inequalities, repeated inequalities and a non-full-dimensional affine hull are allowed; no nondegeneracy or general-position promise is made.

A vertex is an extreme point. A vector \(v\in P\) is a vertex if, for all \(x,y\in P\), the equality \(v=(x+y)/2\) implies \(x=y=v\). Every vertex of a rational polyhedron is rational. The output must contain the coordinate vector of each distinct vertex, exactly once, in arbitrary order, with all \(d\) coordinates in the same reduced rational encoding. It ends with a fixed end marker. An empty polytope produces only that marker. A singleton produces its unique point even if its affine dimension is zero.

Define \(S\) as the sum of the canonical lengths of the distinct required coordinate vectors, including fixed separators and the end marker. Permuting the list does not change its length. Extra padding, duplicate vectors, alternative descriptions of the same vertex and extraneous certificates do not enlarge \(S\). At a vertex, a full-rank selection of active equations determines its coordinates; Cramer’s rule bounds their binary lengths by a polynomial in \(L\). Thus every individual output has polynomial length even though the number of outputs can be exponential.

Use a deterministic multitape Turing machine with bit-operation cost, no advice and no oracle. The same finite program and the same polynomial \(p\) must work for every input satisfying the boundedness promise. Arithmetic precision, preprocessing, writing all coordinates, duplicate handling and the final termination signal are charged. The bound is on total time from start to termination. No polynomial-delay, incremental-polynomial-time or input-polynomial-working-space requirement is added. The algorithm may use space up to its total time bound. Its behavior outside the boundedness promise is immaterial; malformed encodings can be rejected.

context_blocks.text: An inequality system describes a convex region implicitly, while its vertices describe the extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without listing every vertex. The question asks whether converting the whole description requires only polynomial overhead beyond the size of the answer.

A polytope can have exponentially many vertices, so polynomial time in the input alone is not the intended goal. Output-polynomial time allows this unavoidable output cost. It still demands fast termination on instances whose final vertex list is short, even when a natural algorithm encounters a large collection of intermediate objects.

One direct method chooses sets of tight inequalities, solves the resulting linear systems and tests feasibility. Degeneracy can make many different sets identify the same vertex. The total number of bases examined can therefore be much larger than the number of distinct vertices. A total-polynomial bound in the number of such bases would not establish the required output-polynomial bound.

Reimers and Stougie obtain a total-polynomial algorithm when a branch-width parameter of the linear matroid of the constraint matrix is bounded by a fixed constant. This parameter measures how the columns can be recursively divided while limiting the overlap of the spans on either side. Their result supplies a structural tractable case, while their introduction explicitly retains the general bounded-polytope question.

The same source recalls that total-polynomial vertex enumeration for arbitrary unbounded polyhedra would imply P equals NP. Boundedness is therefore a substantive promise. Intersecting an unbounded polyhedron with a large box can introduce additional vertices; the number of these new outputs is not automatically controlled by the original required list, so this operation does not simply transfer the unbounded lower bound.

The arrangement paper, revised in March 2025, enumerates intersections arising throughout a family of hyperplanes. Most such intersections may be infeasible for the chosen orientations of the corresponding inequalities. Its output count can thus be much larger than the number of vertices of one polytope, so enumerating the entire arrangement and filtering it does not give the claimed bound in this card’s output size.

The numerical coordinates are part of the computational model. Their polynomial bit-length bound permits exact rational output and prevents an apparently short geometric answer from hiding unbounded precision costs. Conversely, no compact symbolic description of a vertex replaces the explicitly required coordinate vector.

why: This is a basic unresolved question about converting between implicit and explicit representations of convex feasible regions. A general output-polynomial algorithm would make degeneracy and intermediate representation growth manageable at the level of total complexity, while an impossibility result would separate efficient linear optimization from full exact enumeration.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such an algorithm and polynomial exist, or a proof in Lean of their nonexistence. A positive proof must establish exactness of every rational output, completeness, absence of duplicates, termination and one uniform \(p(L+S)\) bit bound for all bounded rational input polyhedra, including the empty and lower-dimensional cases.

A negative proof must rule out every correct uniform deterministic enumerator with every polynomial total input-plus-output bound. It is not enough to exhibit an input on which a particular pivot rule or intermediate-representation algorithm is slow. A conditional hardness theorem under an unproved complexity assumption is partial progress on this unconditional existence question. Approximate vertices, a fixed dimension, bounded branch-width, nondegeneracy, or enumeration measured against all bases or all arrangement intersections does not meet the full criterion.

importance.reason: A canonical open problem of enumeration complexity connecting polyhedral computation and optimization. The bounded versus unbounded distinction and long-running algorithmic work give it a separate scientific role from counting or approximate optimization.

progress.text: The revised Reimers–Stougie paper gives a total-polynomial algorithm under bounded branch-width and explicitly retains the unrestricted bounded-polytope question.

The arrangement-enumeration work gives algorithms for all intersections of a hyperplane arrangement; version 2 was posted on 25 March 2025. That output set differs from a single polytope’s vertex set.

source_formulation.text: Can the vertices of a bounded polyhedron given by linear inequalities be enumerated in time polynomial in the combined input and output size?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the abstract and opening problem statement, preserving the bounded-polytope target and specifying exact rational output and bit complexity.

sentences: The input describes a bounded rational polyhedron by linear inequalities in variable dimension.
The task is to list every distinct extreme point exactly once and then halt.
The requested total time is polynomial in the combined binary lengths of the input and the required vertex list.
Degeneracy, exponentially many bases per vertex and infeasible arrangement intersections obstruct straightforward enumeration strategies.
An accepted answer proves existence or impossibility of the full uniform algorithm in Lean.
